View PDF View article Google Scholar\n\nResearch paper\n\nExplainable graph neural network for real-time demand states forecasting in water distribution system\n\nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.rineng.2025.106911Get rights and content\n\nUnder a Creative Commons license\n\nOpen access\n\n## Highlights\n\n  * •\n\nAttention-enhanced GNN for real-time demand forecasting based on pressure data.\n\n  * •\n\nModel is independent from hydraulic model, offering broader applicability.\n\n  * •\n\nModel exhibits high spatiotemporal accuracy and sustained long-term effectiveness.\n\n  * •\n\nModel explanation reveals its operational mechanisms, facilitating field deployment.\n\n## Abstract\n\nEfficient real-time nodal demand forecasting in water distribution systems is essential for a reliable and resilient water supply. Given the efficiency of the data-driven approach and the intricate node-line structure of water networks, graph-based machine learning methods offer a promising approach. However, the scarcity of real-time flow acquisition devices limits the ability to directly forecast timely demand. Pressure sensors provide a more practical alternative. Thus, this study proposes a novel attention-augmented gated graph neural network (AGN) for real-time demand forecasting from a pressure perspective. By integrating attention mechanisms, the AGN overcomes limitations of convolution-based graph neural networks, such as capturing long-range dependencies and dynamic node interactions, leading to enhanced performance on real-world modeling problems. This model is formulated for real and sensitive contexts where, in addition to being accurate, the predictions must also be understandable by human operators. Thus, model-level explanations are then introduced in our explainable framework. The proposed AGN outperforms benchmark methods in both spatiotemporal accuracy and long-term forecasting effectiveness, while simultaneously delivering interpretable insights into the demand forecasting process. The novel approach based on the fusion of forecasting and explainability in a single framework enables the creation of powerful and reliable systems suitable for real-world issues and challenges.\n\n## Graphical abstract\n\nImage: Image, graphical abstract\n\n  1. Download: Download high-res image (273KB)\n  2. Download: Download full-size image\n\n  * Previous article in issue\n  * Next article in issue\n\n## Keywords\n\nExplainability\n\nReal-time\n\nDemand forecasting\n\nAttention mechanisms\n\nGraph neural network\n\nWater distribution system\n\n## 1. Introduction\n\nAs urban populations and city sizes continue to grow, urban water distribution systems (WDSs), as a fundamental component for ensuring public welfare, are facing increasing complexity and management challenges [10,25]. To maintain the stability of WDSs, accurate forecasting and proactive preparation for future demands are essential [11,35]. The predictive lead time establishes critical temporal buffers for municipal water operators, strengthening their operational resilience. However, short-term demand forecasting in real-life WDSs proves challenging due to the need for predictions at all nodes based on limited sensor layouts and complex network topology. Achieving real-time efficient forecasting based on the hydraulic model seems unattainable, especially for cities lacking a hydraulic model. Consequently, the primary objective of this study focuses on developing an innovative state estimation framework that operates independently of conventional hydraulic modeling paradigms.\n\nSeveral studies [18,33,37] have enabled direct modeling of WDSs, obviating the need for hydraulic models. Based on the assumption of smooth variations in nodal head (the sum of nodal pressure and elevation of a node), Zhou et al. [37] developed a graph-based head reconstruction (GHR) method. This method decomposes the hydraulic head into components with different variation speeds, reconstructing the head using the slowly varying components obtained from a limited number of monitoring nodes. However, this method heavily relies on having a sufficient number of well-defined sensor nodes and a regular underlying graph structure. Xing and Sela [33] were the pioneers in employing a graph neural network (GNN) to achieve state estimation within WDSs. They developed an encoder-decoder GNN architecture, enabling real-time synchronous estimation of pipeline flow and nodal pressure states. Their research demonstrated the robustness of the GNN model to various levels of noise. By applying the gated graph neural network (GGNN), Li et al. [18] were the first to achieve the state forecasting for water quality. The GGNN algorithm, derived from gated recurrent unit (GRU), was applied for the first time in the domain of the WDS, yielding promising spatiotemporal predictive outputs. Although the aforementioned methods can be used for predicting future water demand states, they still have limitations. The methods in the first two studies were limited to estimating the current state. While integrating time series prediction algorithms with their methods could achieve future state forecasting, the simple stacking of time series forecasting and state estimation would lead to error accumulation. The GGNN method offers a novel approach to developing alternative models for state forecasting in WDSs. However, directly applying the GGNN method does not tightly integrate with the characteristics of water networks. Additionally, GGNN requires recurrent graph convolution operations to expand the receptive field, which limits its application in large-scale pipe networks and leads to over-smoothing issues.\n\nDespite excellent results and a broad range of applications, GNN models are still treated as black boxes [16]: the underlying mechanisms that steer the learning process and generalization ability remain a challenging and open question [29]. Merely achieving good performance is not enough to guarantee the deployment of models in production [13,21], especially in critical operational contexts where additional performance metrics such as robustness or safety are paramount. In such environments, human operators must comprehend and trust the model's predictions. Also, a deeper understanding of the model would improve its predictive performance [22]. Therefore, the second goal of this paper is to explain the results generated by the model.\n\nThis study innovative proposes an explainable attention-augmented gated graph neural network (AGN) framework for water demand states forecasting from a pressure perspective. Derived from GRU-based GNN (i.e. GGNN), this model not only exhibits excellent time series prediction performance but also captures the network’s structure. The innovative attention mechanisms are then incorporated to address the limitation of GGNN in capturing solely local dependencies and enhance the model's interpretability through its transparent decision-making process. Overall, the paper encompasses the following novelties:\n\n·Demand forecasting model designed for water network characteristics: A core innovation of this study is the development of the AGN model, specifically designed to capture the unique spatio-temporal characteristics of water distribution networks. The proposed AGN model forecasts future demands at all nodes, without relying on hydraulic models. The AGN model shows significant accuracy in both spatial and temporal dimensions compared to existing direct modeling methods. The model maintains high predictive robustness across various forecasting horizons. Our high accuracy results validate the feasibility and efficiency of demand prediction from a pressure perspective.\n\nModel explanation associated with water network characteristics: Merely achieving sufficient prediction accuracy is not enough to guarantee the model’s deployment in real-world WDSs. To bridge this gap, the second innovation addresses the crucial need for improved model transparency. Specifically, the key lies in integrating model explanations with practical engineering issues, enabling network managers to understand and trust the model, thereby making reliable decisions. To the best knowledge, we are the first to address interpretability issues in WDS. By providing these explanations, this study provided a deeper understanding of the roles of different model components in the prediction task. This process also aids in improving the model by offering feedback to further enhance its predictive performance.\n\n## 2. Methodology\n\nThis study proposes an Attentive Graph Network (AGN) to forecast water demand in distribution systems using pressure data without hydraulic modeling. The architecture leverages the inherent graph structure of water networks, historical pressure measurements, and nodal features to predict future nodal demands. Specifically designed to capture unique pressure characteristics in water distribution systems (WDS), the model includes built-in interpretability mechanisms to ensure transparency. The following sections detail the challenges addressed and present the explainable AGN framework.\n\n### 2.1. Problem formulation\n\nBefore discussing the issues and challenges, this study provide a detailed introduction to the symbolic representation of WDS as a graph. The WDS is represented as an undirected graph \\mathcal{G}=\\left(\\mathcal{V},\\mathcal{E},\\mathcal{W}\\right). Here, \\mathcal{V} is the set of I+{I}^{*} vertices representing nodes that comprise reservoirs, tanks and junctions. \\mathcal{E} is the set of edges representing the valves, pumps, and pipes. \\mathcal{W}\\in {\\mathbb{R}}^{\\left(I+{I}^{*}\\right)\\times \\left(I+{I}^{*}\\right)} is the weighted adjacency matrix. ### 2.2. Explainable forecasting framework\n\nThe GRU [6] is a highly optimized variant of the recurrent neural network. Its core advantage lies in its unique architectural design. Through the precise regulatory mechanisms of the update gate and reset gate, the GRU skillfully balances the retention and forgetting of historical information [7]. This allows it to capture the dynamics of long-term and short-term dependencies in time series data [24]. The GGNN, an innovative extension of the GRU [17], integrates recurrent layers, graph convolution, and gating mechanisms. It retains the advantages of the GRU in time series prediction while deeply analyzing the complex structure of non-Euclidean space graph data through graph convolution operations, achieving efficient utilization of graph data [31]. However, the GGNN also faces limitations of the convolution-based graph methods: Each iteration only focuses on the first-order neighborhood of the sensor nodes. Thus, the iteration of the recurrent layers restricts the generalization of sensor node features to a larger network space [32].\n\nBuilding upon the dynamic global weighting capability of attention mechanisms, this study enhances the GGNN framework by integrating self-attention and external-attention modules. The self-attention module addresses the limited ability of standard graph convolutions to capture long-range spatial dependencies among nodes, significantly improving spatial representational capacity. The external-attention module explicitly models the relationships between nodal attributes and pressure observations, enhancing the model's physical relevance to WDSs. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall AGN architecture. The subsequent sections detail the design and implementation of this framework:\n\nImage: Fig 1\n\n  1. First, this study report and analyze the forecasting task results: the proposed method achieves superior spatial generalization and temporal forecasting accuracy compared to previous approaches. Subsequently, this study evaluates the robustness of the AGN model across varying prediction windows. Methodology\n\nThis transfer learning approach utilizes monitored information from both the source WDN G_{s} and the target WDN G_{t} to learn a model capable of accurately estimating the remaining node pressures in the target WDN. (2025). Here, N_{s} denotes the total number of nodes in the source WDN. If there is an edge between nodes n_{i} and n_{j}, A_{s,i,j} = 1; otherwise, A_{s,i,j} = 0. To effectively encode the structural information from both WDNs and extract meaningful node representations for downstream tasks (Wang et al., 2025); (2) Shift Parameters. Shift parameters are introduced to reduce differences in hydraulic characteristics, topology, and sensor deployment between the source and target WDNs (Qiao et al., 2024), and they are trained within the source feature extraction process to better align the source WDN with the target; (3) Graph Laplacian Regularization. To address pressure data scarcity, Graph Laplacian regularization enforces smoothness in predicted values across adjacent nodes (Singh and Chakraborty, 2020), thereby enhancing the stability of pressure estimation. This method leverages the local graph topology to enhance accuracy while preserving the intrinsic structure of the target WDN.\n\nImage: Fig 1\n\n  1. Download: Download high-res image (602KB)\n  2. The architecture of GASTL.\n\nNotably, for the same topology, compared with “L-Town to C-Town” transfer, all four metrics show significant improvement, with MAE reduced from 36.55 m to 22.47 m and MAPE dropping from 34.94 % to 26.26 %. This suggests that within the same topology, structural similarities facilitate transfer learning, whereas topological differences hinder effective knowledge transfer.\n\nOur proposed transfer learning approach with three Heter-GATRes blocks and achieves the lowest MAE of 7.31 m (C-Town to C-Town and L-Town to C-Town) and MAPE of 9.15 % (C-Town to C-Town) and 9.43 % (L-Town to C-Town), outperforming all baseline methods. Under noisy conditions, GASTL still achieves an R² of 0.88, reaching a level suitable for practical application. Increasing the number of Hetero-GATRes blocks (GASTL 10 blocks) does not yield further improvements, indicating the risk of overfitting issues in Source WDNs. Additionally, the No Shift model produces results comparable to GASTL (3 blocks), but in the same topology, R² (0.91) and RMSE (10.25 m) of No Shift perform better, whereas in L-Town to C-Town, MAE (7.23 m) and MAPE (9.32 %) are higher. This suggests that in the same topology, shift parameters make cross-domain alignment more challenging, while in different topologies, they provide better adaptation.\n\n## 6. Conclusions\n\nThis study investigated a critical problem of pressure estimation in a scarcely monitored WDN through transfer learning from a well-monitored source WDN. We propose GASTL, an approach that leverages shift parameters and Graph Laplacian regularization to enhance model transferability. Through this study, the main conclusions are as follows:\n\n  * 1.\n\nGASTL demonstrates robust performance in both Same-topology and Cross-topology transfer scenarios. Owing to structural consistency, Same-topology transfer better preserves local hydraulic patterns, resulting in slightly improved MAE and MAPE. In contrast, structural differences in Cross-topology settings encourage global pattern generalization, leading to higher R² and lower RMSE.\n\n  * 2.\n\nSensor placement and quantity in the target WDN directly affect pressure coverage, which in turn impacts transfer performance. Insufficient or uneven sensor distribution can lead to limited pressure coverage, resulting in information loss and reduced adaptation effectiveness.\n\n  * 3.\n\nFeature alignment techniques, such as shift parameter adaptation and Graph Laplacian regularization, enhance transferability by mitigating topological discrepancies. However, data noise and substantial pressure distribution differences between source and target WDNs remain key challenges that can affect transfer accuracy.\n\nWith the increasing availability of public WDN datasets, transfer learning presents new opportunities for efficient pressure estimation. However, not all WDNs are suitable as knowledge sources, and improper transfer selection may introduce noise, leading to negative transfer effects. Image: Request Full-text Paper PDF\n\n# Leak Detection and Localization in Water Distribution Networks Using Conditional Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks\n\n  * April 2023\n  * Water Research 238(2):120012\n\nDOI:10.1016/j.watres.2023.120012\n\nAuthors:\n\nMohammad Mahdi Rajabi\n\nMohammad Mahdi Rajabi\n\n  * This person is not on ResearchGate, or hasn't claimed this research yet.\n\nPooya Komeilian\n\n  * University of North Florida\n\nXi Wan\n\n  * University of Exeter\n\nRaziyeh Farmani\n\n  * University of Exeter\n\nImage: Request Full-text Paper PDF\n\nRequest full-text PDF\n\nTo read the full-text of this research, you can request a copy directly from the authors.\n\n## Abstract\n\nThis paper explores the use of 'conditional convolutional generative adversarial networks' (CDCGAN) for image-based leak detection and localization (LD&L) in water distribution networks (WDNs). The method employs pressure measurements and is based on four pillars: (1) hydraulic model-based generation of leak-free training data by taking into account the demand uncertainty, (2) conversion of hydraulic model input demand-output pressure pairs into images using kriging interpolation, (3) training of a CDCGAN model for image-to-image translation, and (4) using the structural similarity (SSIM) index for LD&L. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n(PDF) Development and validation of a high-performance liquid chromatography method with fluorescence detection for the quantification of the resistance protein P-gp in cancer cells (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388236321_Development_and_validation_of_a_high-performance_liquid_chromatography_method_with_fluorescence_detection_for_the_quantification_of_the_resistance_protein_P-gp_in_cancer_cells)\nciteturn20search3 [wordlim: 200] Published: 1.6 years ago; Crawled: 5 months ago; Journal of Chromatography B 1253 (2025) 124475 ... the work reported in this paper. ... Télécharger le format pdf\nSelon cet article « Les associations dont le budget annuel est supérieur à 150 000 euros et recevant une ou plusieurs subventions de l'État ou d'une collectivité territoriale dont le montant est supérieur à 50 000 euros doivent publier chaque année dans le compte financier les rémunérations des trois plus hauts cadres dirigeants bénévoles et salariés ainsi que leurs avantages en nature. » Une disposition analogue oblige, d'ores et déjà, les associations qui décident de verser une rémunération à leurs dirigeants, dans les conditions prévues au d du 1° du 7 de l'article 261 du code général des impôts, d'inscrire le montant des rémunérations versées à chacun des dirigeants concernés « dans une annexe aux comptes de l'organisme ». L'objectif du législateur, pour reprendre l'exposé des motifs de l'amendement parlementaire à l'origine de cette disposition, est de renforcer « la transparence de la gestion des fonds publics ». Ainsi, pour l'application de ce texte, il convient de considérer qu'une association doit publier, dans une annexe de ses comptes, « les rémunérations des trois plus hauts cadres dirigeants bénévoles et salariés ainsi que leurs avantages en nature », dès lors qu'elle dispose d'un budget annuel supérieur à 150 000 euros et bénéficie, de la part d'une ou plusieurs collectivités publiques, d'une subvention ou de plusieurs subventions dont le montant cumulé est supérieur à 50 000 euros. S'agissant, enfin, de la détermination de l'année de référence visée à l'article 20 de la loi précitée, il convient de prendre en compte l'exercice au cours duquel le versement de la ou des subventions a été effectué.\n\nTélécharger le format pdf\n\nDonnées clés\n\n* * *\n\nAuteur : Mme Sylvie Andrieux\n\nType de question : Question écrite\n\nRubrique : Associations\n\nMinistère interrogé : jeunesse et sports\n\nMinistère répondant : jeunesse et sports\n\nDates :\nQuestion publiée le 17 octobre 2006\nRéponse publiée le 16 janvier 2007\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nSmart Water Futures: designing the next generation of urban drinking water systems | Water-Futures | Progetto | Risultati | H2020 | CORDIS | Commissione europea (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/951424/results/it)\nciteturn20search8 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week;
